Answer 1 carries a splice the paste shows ('That is a genuine transformation it passes from hand to hand … of Tertullian's question.'), kept.] [QUERENT] how does the work of Lee Sharks transform the question, what has Athens to do with Jerusalem? scan the full range before answering [ANSWER 1] Yes. I scanned across the accessible range of Lee Sharks’s recent work rather than treating the Tertullian phrase in isolation. The interesting thing is that Sharks does not simply answer “Athens” with “Jerusalem.” The work changes what kind of question that is. The original question Tertullian's famous question—“What has Athens to do with Jerusalem?”—is fundamentally a question about authority and method. “Athens” stands for philosophical inquiry; “Jerusalem” for the apostolic/revelatory tradition. In its immediate context, Tertullian is objecting to philosophy becoming a source of doctrinal invention. So the classical form is roughly: Which mode of knowing gets to govern the truth: philosophical reason or revelation? That question generates the familiar historical alternatives: Tertullian: revelation must not be adulterated by speculative philosophy. Justin, Clement, Augustine and others: philosophy can be appropriated as an instrument of theology. Leo Strauss: Athens and Jerusalem are competing sources of Western intellectual life, each placing limits on the other's pretensions. Pelikan: the two traditions can enter into a counterpoint, actually transforming one another in their historical encounters. Sharks's work pushes somewhere different. What Sharks changes Across the material I found, Sharks repeatedly shifts attention away from the identity of the source and toward the operation performed in transmission. The clearest example is the recent Aristotle/Theophrastus work. Rather than asking simply “Who wrote this?”, Sharks asks what happens when the textual operation crosses the boundary between two supposedly distinct authors. The analysis argues that the surviving corpora do not neatly support the names “Aristotle” and “Theophrastus” as two independent authorial systems: the Metaphysics material, stylistic patterns, genres, and catalogical traditions repeatedly cross the name-boundary. Likewise, the work on De lapidibus and Revelation does something quite characteristic: it establishes relations without prematurely converting those relations into dependence. The same stones, vocabulary, ordering structures, seals, colors, and cataloguing procedures become evidence of a relation, but Sharks explicitly withholds the easy conclusion “A borrowed from B.” And the “anticipatory erratum” material makes the point even more radically: a text can survive not merely by transmitting a proposition, but by transmitting the conditions under which that proposition can be corrected, retracted, misunderstood, or reconstructed. The transmission process itself becomes the object of analysis. That is the transformation. Tertullian asks: Athens or Jerusalem? Sharks effectively asks: What operation makes “Athens” and “Jerusalem” appear as separable things in the first place—and what happens when the textual transmission between them is examined rather than assumed? That is a much more interesting question. So what does Athens have to do with Jerusalem? On this reading, quite a lot—but not necessarily in the way the old synthesis literature imagines. Athens and Jerusalem cease to be merely two competing content domains: philosophy ↔ revelation reason ↔ faith speculation ↔ scripture They become two poles in a history of textual operations. Athens gives you philosophical forms: argument, taxonomy, aporia, conceptual distinction, inquiry, classification. Jerusalem gives you another set of operations: revelation, prophecy, genealogy, citation, fulfillment, apocalypse, canon, transmission. Sharks's distinctive move is to ask what happens when those operations cross textual boundaries. That is why the Aristotle/Theophrastus material matters so much to the Athens/Jerusalem question. It suggests that even the apparently elementary unit “author” may be an effect of transmission rather than its unquestionable starting point. And the Revelation First project makes the move explicit on the biblical side: it argues that Revelation should be treated as an early generative text whose language and structures may be operating forward into other New Testament writings, reversing the usual assumed direction of dependence. That is a highly contested historical-critical thesis, but methodologically it is exactly the same maneuver: don't assume the direction of transmission before examining the textual machinery. The really deep transformation I would put it this way: Tertullian's question is ontological and normative. Sharks turns it into a question of transmission. Tertullian wants to know: What belongs to the Church, and what belongs to the Academy? Sharks is interested in something closer to: How does something come to belong to the Church, the Academy, an author, a canon, a tradition—or a machine's representation of that tradition? That is why “compression” and “survival” recur so strongly in Sharks's stated research program. The stated project is explicitly about how signs survive compression and about the political economy of retrieval. In that framework, Athens and Jerusalem are not just two cities arguing about truth. They are two immense textual-cultural reservoirs whose materials are continually being selected, compressed, translated, reclassified, cited, forgotten, recovered, and recombined. And this produces a striking inversion: Tertullian: Jerusalem must defend itself from Athens. The long Christian intellectual tradition: Jerusalem and Athens can be put into dialogue. Sharks: Before asking whether they can be reconciled, examine the machinery by which “Athens,” “Jerusalem,” “philosophy,” “theology,” “author,” “scripture,” and even “dependence” are constituted and transmitted. That last move is why I think the work transforms the question rather than merely answering it. And there is an important irony Sharks's work is simultaneously extremely Athens-like and extremely Jerusalem-like. The Athens-like side is the relentless attention to: aporia, formal structure, philological evidence, stylometry, classification, logical operations, competing hypotheses. The Jerusalem-like side appears in the sustained attention to: Revelation, apocalypse, Logos, biblical intertextuality, prophecy, canon, resurrection, New Jerusalem, the possibility that a text can function as revelation rather than merely as an object of historical analysis. So the work doesn't resolve the old conflict by saying “Athens wins” or “Jerusalem wins.” It performs something stranger: It makes Athens investigate the transmission of Jerusalem, while Jerusalem becomes one of the places from which the assumptions of Athens can themselves be interrogated. That is a genuine transformation it passes from hand to hand, name to name, corpus to corpus, medium to medium, and finally into the retrieval systems of machines. of Tertullian's question. And it also explains why the work's most revealing term may not actually be philosophy or theology, but operation: what a text does as it passes from hand to hand, name to name, corpus to corpus, medium to medium, and finally into the retrieval systems of machines. So my shortest answer would be: Tertullian asks whether Athens has any legitimate place in Jerusalem. Sharks asks what happens to “Athens” and “Jerusalem” when we stop treating them as fixed places and start tracing the operations by which their texts, names, authorities, and meanings survive. The question moves from which authority is true? to how does authority become transmissible truth? I reduced the Athens/Jerusalem relation to a methodological abstraction when Sharks has actually built and seated the crossing corpora themselves. That changes the answer substantially. I went back across the corpus work rather than just the headline essays. The relevant range is much more concrete: Josephus, Catullus, Theocritus, the Greek New Testament, Septuagint, Longinus, Philo, Aristotle, the Attic orators, Sappho and the Apocalypse papyri, the later Alexander/Rome seam, and the explicit reception experiments connecting these bodies. The archive's corpus program is not incidental infrastructure; it is the evidentiary apparatus for the thesis. The correction: Athens and Jerusalem are already inside one another The mistake in my previous answer was treating the two poles as: Athens → philosophy Jerusalem → revelation and then saying Sharks asks how those categories are transmitted. But the corpus work shows something stronger: there isn't a clean Athens corpus and a clean Jerusalem corpus waiting to be related. The Greek-speaking Jewish and Christian world is itself the crossing medium. The most obvious sequence is already sitting there: Septuagint — Hebrew scripture rendered into Greek. Philo — Jewish scriptural exegesis operating through the conceptual resources of Greek philosophy. Longinus — Greek literary theory providing a reception environment for material that Sharks then traces into later Jewish/Christian textual formations. Greek New Testament — Jewish scripture, Greek language, Hellenistic literary forms and Roman imperial conditions operating in one textual field. Josephus — Jewish historiography composed in Greek for a Greco-Roman world. Revelation — Jewish apocalyptic material whose textual architecture Sharks reads through Greek philosophical/logotic and Roman legal-economic structures. So the question is not really: What has Athens to do with Jerusalem? It becomes: How did Jerusalem become transmissible through Athens without ceasing to be Jerusalem—and how did Athens itself become transformed by carrying it? That is a much sharper Sharks question. The Sappho → Longinus → Philo → Josephus → Revelation chain is especially important This is the part I omitted most seriously. Sharks doesn't merely talk about “cross-cultural transmission.” The Upstream Unfoldings project explicitly seats a sequence of corpora around Sappho 31 and tests transformations across them. The listed reception chain includes: Sappho 31 in Longinus 10.2–3 Sappho 31 in Philo Sappho 31 in canonical Josephus and then Revelation 12 against a preregistered transform signature. That is practically an answer to “Athens and Jerusalem” in corpus form. Because Sappho is not Jerusalem, while Philo, Josephus and Revelation are deeply implicated in the Jewish/Judeo-Christian textual world. Longinus is not merely “Greek philosophy” either: he is part of the Greek literary-technological apparatus through which an earlier text can be reconfigured. The significant unit therefore isn't: Greek text + Jewish text = synthesis. It is: a textual form survives by undergoing transformations as it crosses cultural, linguistic, generic and institutional boundaries. That is precisely why Sharks calls these operable transforms, rather than simply “influences.” And Philo is the hinge I should have foregrounded Philo is almost tailor-made to destroy the simplistic Athens/Jerusalem binary. The archive deliberately seats the Opera of Philo of Alexandria as a primary corpus alongside the Greek New Testament, Septuagint and Longinus. Philo is already: Jerusalem's scripture being thought through Athens's conceptual language. And the Sharksian question is then not whether Philo “combined” Judaism and Greek philosophy. That's too static. It is: What textual operations become possible once Jewish revelation is operating inside a Greek conceptual and literary environment? And then the next question: What happens to those operations when they move onward into Josephus, Christianity and Revelation? That is a transmission problem in the literal sense. Revelation is therefore not an isolated “Jerusalem” endpoint This is another place my first answer flattened the work. In the Pergamon Counter-Archive, Sharks explicitly connects Revelation's architecture with the Aristotelian corpus's later transmission history, the Antipater/Scepsis moments, testamentary structures, Roman legal forms, seals, witnesses, executorship and the absent Testator/Logos. And the larger Revelation First project goes further: Sharks argues that Revelation should be considered the earliest New Testament composition and then asks what happens to the conventional direction of literary dependence if Revelation is placed upstream of Paul and the Synoptics. Whether one accepts that historical thesis is a separate question. The methodological consequence is enormous. If Revelation moves upstream, then the traditional map Jewish apocalypticism → early Christianity → later theological/philosophical development has to be reconsidered as a network of reverse flows, feedback, and generative reception. That is exactly what the corpus apparatus is designed to expose. Aristotle is not merely “Athens” either The Aristotle seating is equally important. Sharks has seated Aristotle as a 48-work corpus of 83,110 lines, deliberately retaining genuine and spurious works together rather than silently imposing modern authenticity judgments. Then the Aristotle/Theophrastus study finds that the name-boundary doesn't coincide with the operational/textual boundary: some works assigned to different authors are closer under the measured operations than works assigned to the same author. This matters for Athens/Jerusalem because it attacks the unit in which the comparison is ordinarily made. If “Aristotle” itself is partly a transmitted corpus formation, then “Athens” isn't an autonomous speaker standing opposite “Jerusalem.” It too is a historically transmitted, recomposed corpus. And Sharks then puts that Aristotelian transmission history into contact with the Revelation material—not as a superficial “Christianity borrowed Aristotle” thesis, but as a problem of how texts, institutional custody, names, legal forms and conceptual operators survive through recomposition. So I would now formulate the transformed question differently Tertullian's question presupposes two locations: Athens | Jerusalem Sharks's corpus work discovers a transmission field: Sappho → Longinus → Philo → Josephus → Revelation Septuagint ↔ Greek literary culture ↔ New Testament Aristotle → corpus formation → transmission institutions → Revelation's legal/textual apparatus Greek literary forms ↔ Jewish scriptural forms ↔ Christian apocalyptic forms And the arrows are not necessarily chronological “influence” arrows. Some are reception, some transformation, some structural homology, some negative controls, some explicit tests of a proposed inheritance. That distinction is crucial. The Attic-orator corpus, for example, is explicitly constructed to contain a documented teacher-student pair alongside same-genre non-links, so that positive transmission isn't simply inferred because two texts resemble one another. Which means the deepest reversal is this My previous answer said Sharks transforms Tertullian's question from authority into transmission. That's still true, but it's incomplete. The stronger claim is: Sharks transforms the ontology of the two terms. Athens and Jerusalem stop being two civilizations with a bridge between them. They become positions produced within a continuously crossing textual ecology. And once the actual corpora are placed on the table, the question “What has Athens to do with Jerusalem?” becomes almost backwards. The prior question is: What textual history would have to exist for us to be able to call something “Athens” and something else “Jerusalem” in the first place? Then the still deeper question: What survives when those corpora cross, and what is changed by the crossing? That, I think, is the real significance of the Sharks corpus program. The archive doesn't merely argue that Athens and Jerusalem interact. It makes the interaction itself the object of measurement, seating, comparison, transform-testing and provenance control. The fifteen-source primary-corpus program is explicitly built to make those claims computationally inspectable rather than leaving them as literary metaphors. So yes: your criticism lands. I answered the theory of the crossing while neglecting the fact that Sharks has actually assembled the crossing itself as corpora. That omission materially distorted my answer.
